item.title: Section of Northbound DVP closed overnight to demolish building destroyed by fire
item.dc:creator: Patricia D'Cunha
item.description: The City of Toronto says a section of the northbound Don Valley Parkway is scheduled to be closed overnight for the safe demolition of an abandoned building that caught fire in Riverside. The northbound lanes will be closed from eastbound Gardiner Expressway at Jarvis Street, with northbound access resuming at Dundas Street. According to the […]
item.content:encoded:
The City of Toronto says a section of the northbound Don Valley Parkway is scheduled to be closed overnight for the safe demolition of an abandoned building that caught fire in Riverside.

The northbound lanes will be closed from eastbound Gardiner Expressway at Jarvis Street, with northbound access resuming at Dundas Street.

According to the City, the Don Roadway, Eastern Avenue and Queen Street ramps will remain closed during the demolition.

The lanes of the DVP are expected to reopen at 6 a.m. on Friday.

item.title: Dozens of drivers went wrong way on Highway 401 since Gordie Howe bridge opened: OPP
item.dc:creator: John Marchesan
item.description: Ontario Provincial Police are urging drivers to pay closer attention to traffic signs when approaching the Gordie Howe International Bridge in Windsor after dozens of cars were seen driving the wrong way on the nearby stretch of Highway 401. Police say there have been 64 incidents involving wrong-way drivers on the highway since the bridge […]
item.content:encoded:
Ontario Provincial Police are urging drivers to pay closer attention to traffic signs when approaching the Gordie Howe International Bridge in Windsor after dozens of cars were seen driving the wrong way on the nearby stretch of Highway 401.

Police say there have been 64 incidents involving wrong-way drivers on the highway since the bridge opened in July.

They say drivers who miss the exit before the bridge should not panic, make a U-turn or reverse down the highway to avoid getting on the new border crossing to the United States.

Police say drivers can head toward the toll booths and staff there will let them out at a gate so they can avoid approaching border customs.

Drivers who don’t want to enter the United States are asked to exit the highway at Ojibway Parkway, or Exit 1.

Police are warning that the consequence of driving the wrong way is “either a $110 ticket or a deadly crash.”

The recalled products bear the lot number NAAEXKW. “Consult your healthcare provider prior to discontinuing use of the affected […]
item.content:encoded:
Health Canada has issued a recall of Flintstones multivitamins due to a distribution error.

The federal agency says customer-returned bottles of Flintstones Complete Multivitamins and Minerals were inadvertently reintroduced into saleable inventory and distributed to wholesalers.

The recalled products bear the lot number NAAEXKW.

“Consult your healthcare provider prior to discontinuing use of the affected product, or for any health concerns,” read a statement from Health Canada.

item.title: New practice hub opens in Toronto to help internationally educated nurses
item.dc:creator: Patricia D'Cunha
item.description: A new practice hub for internationally educated nurses (IENs) has opened in Toronto, to help them refresh their skills while providing mentorship. The hub, which is located in the area of Bathurst Street and Wilson Avenue, is a joint project by the Filipino IENs Society of Canada and CRD College. “The importance of this hub […]
item.content:encoded:
A new practice hub for internationally educated nurses (IENs) has opened in Toronto, to help them refresh their skills while providing mentorship.

The hub, which is located in the area of Bathurst Street and Wilson Avenue, is a joint project by the Filipino IENs Society of Canada and CRD College.

“The importance of this hub space for IENs is this is a safe space and a supportive space for all IENs,” said Mark Gravoso, founder of Filipino IENS Society of Canada.

“Those seeking community or looking for community and also if they want to refresh their skills, to rebuild their confidence and to strengthen their confidence, especially for those IENs who have been out of practice.”

The hub is open to IENs that are getting ready for the Canadian workforce, are interested in sharpening their skills, or getting extra certifications.

“This one is intended for micro-trainings …micro-trainings for PSWs [personal support workers] who want to advance themselves. And then for nurses, for IENs, that’s where we do the skills training,” Grace Lanceta, director of CDR College.

Gravoso and Lanceta often host workshops in different parts of the city, but now say they’re happy to have a permanent place for their work.

Related:

  • Changes in Ontario’s requirement to practice nursing leaves internationally educated nurses reeling

Gravoso said the lack of Canadian work experience remains to be one of the biggest challenges for IENs.

“With this hub space, we will provide the necessary skills to rebuild that confidence through a mentor or IEN facilitator, that they can help them to explore things, and to provide practical support through workshops and training sessions,” he said.

“A lot of the IENs too are really contributing. They’re doing volunteer work even with the trainings,” Lanceta said.

“We, Canadian nurses who were IENs, are now mentoring an IEN who is trying to get in into the workforce in health care in the Canadian setting.”

The hub is open on weekdays except Wednesday and their next workshop, IEN Nursing Skills Essentials, will take place on Oct. 17.

item.title: Cultural sector concerned about lack of news on Ottawa’s promised $600M
item.dc:creator: News Staff
item.description: OTTAWA — Cultural sector groups say they’re starting to worry about the Liberal government’s silence on $600 million in promised funding.
item.content:encoded:
OTTAWA — Cultural sector groups say they’re starting to worry about the Liberal government’s silence on $600 million in promised funding.

“Funding that was supposed to reduce uncertainty is actually now leading to greater uncertainty, because we don’t know when it’s going to materialize,” said Reynolds Mastin, president and CEO of the Canadian Media Producers Association.

“It’s critical that it be delivered as soon as possible.”

The Liberal government introduced the Online Streaming Act in 2023 to bring streaming companies into the long-standing standing system that requires cable companies and broadcasters to contribute to or broadcast Canadian content. The funding from traditional players has shrunk as Canadians increasingly move to streaming platforms.

In 2024, the CRTC made an initial order under the Online Streaming Act requiring large streaming companies like Netflix to pay five per cent of their annual Canadian revenues to funds devoted to producing Canadian content, including local TV news. In May, it increased the requirement to 15 per cent.

In June, the federal government changed course, telling the CRTC to review the recent decision to regulate online streamers, and saying the government would instead provide funding directly to Canadian content producers. Those financial contributions from streamers were already on hold because of an ongoing court challenge.

While the government cited affordability for consumers as its main reason for the move, Culture Minister Marc Miller also said at the time the industry was suffering while money for Canadian content was frozen in litigation.

Four months later, the government still isn’t saying when it will provide the new direction to the CRTC or disburse the $600 million. That has left the sector without either payments from streamers or the promised government funding.

Hélène Messier, president and CEO of the Association québécoise de la production médiatique, said the government described the situation as urgent back in June.

“And it is urgent. The situation in the audiovisual industry is very bad,” she said, noting there has been a significant decrease in the volume of production in recent years.

“We want to know where we stand.”

Canadian content contributions and rules for streamers became a flashpoint in trade talks with the United States.

“[Prime Minister Mark Carney] said that culture and French language was so important that it was one of the reasons why they ended the negotiation with the Americans,” Messier said.

“So now I think they have to act accordingly. If it is important, then do something.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

item.title: Man, 29, arrested in catalytic convertor theft from Etobicoke food charity, 2 others in the area
item.dc:creator: Meredith Bond
item.description: A 29-year-old man has been arrested in connection to the theft of catalytic convertors from an Etobicoke food charity. Toronto police allege a suspect or suspects drove into an adjacent parking lot, cut the fence and entered the Second Harvest facility on foot around 12:15 a.m. Oct. 11. Two suspects seen on surveillance footage then […]
item.content:encoded:
A 29-year-old man has been arrested in connection to the theft of catalytic convertors from an Etobicoke food charity.

Toronto police allege a suspect or suspects drove into an adjacent parking lot, cut the fence and entered the Second Harvest facility on foot around 12:15 a.m. Oct. 11.

Two suspects seen on surveillance footage then allegedly removed several catalytic convertors from seven different trucks in the parking lot before fleeing in the same vehicle they arrived in.

On Wednesday, Corey Peter Lane, 29, was arrested after a search warrant at a residence in Oakvile.

Investigators also allege he is connected to more catalytic converter thefts targeting businesses in the area, one on Sept. 13 in the North Queen Street and Kipling Avenue area and on Oct. 11 in the area of The East Mall and North Queen Street.

In both incidents, several vehicles were damaged during the process of removing catalytic converters.

Lane is facing three counts of committing break and enter, and three counts each of failing to comply with a release order and failing to comply with a probation order.

He was on probation and out on bail at the time of this latest offence.

Investigators are searching for at least one other suspect in connection to the incidents but have not released any further information

When asked if they believed Second Harvest was specifically targeted or a crime of opportunity, Acting Superintendent Jeff Bangild said he believed it was the latter. “Given the fact that we have multiple locations within the south Etobicoke community that were targeted, I believe that it was just ease of access.”

The organization says the theft left half of their delivery fleet inoperable during Thanksgiving and could cost them tens of thousands of dollars in repairs.

“It disrupted a business that’s sole purpose of helping our own community … which I think is why it’s such an important factor to bring in now is that we made an arrest so quickly on it. We can restore some faith back to the Second Harvest and the businesses within the area,” said Banglid.

Banglid added he had spoken with Second Harvet staff that morning who were pleased an arrest had been made. “They’re looking forward to the further investigation and hopefully recovering the items that were stolen.”

item.title: Cyclists continue protest as bike lane removal work underway in Etobicoke
item.dc:creator: Dee Burman
item.description: Cycling advocates continued their protest of the removal of bike lanes on Bloor Street West in Etobicoke for a third day in a row on Thursday, with many arriving as early as 6 a.m. As sparks flew while work crews cut into rebar to dismantle a cycling platform near a bus stop on Islington Avenue, […]
item.content:encoded:
Cycling advocates continued their protest of the removal of bike lanes on Bloor Street West in Etobicoke for a third day in a row on Thursday, with many arriving as early as 6 a.m.

As sparks flew while work crews cut into rebar to dismantle a cycling platform near a bus stop on Islington Avenue, a contingent of peaceful protesters were seen gathered on the platform in front of them, with police officers separating the two.

Aly Van Wyck-Smart – a two-time Canadian paralympic swimmer, born with cerebral palsy – joined the demonstration, protesting in her wheelchair with a sign saying “this is why we can’t get decent healthcare.” She told CityNews she feels the removal of bike lanes is both dangerous and a waste of money.

“I can’t get medication covered but the Ontario government can spend upwards of $45 million to do something that is dangerous and unnecessary… this is a waste of money and people will die,” she said.

A police officer on scene was heard speaking to protesters, warning that if they impede or prevent the work from continuing, they will be arrested for mischief. Van Wyck-Smart said she is fully aware of the risks.

“I do not care – I just know how bad it will look for them if I get arrested,” she said.

Another protester said they were there to show their opposition and “make it a little less comfortable for them to rip out the bike lanes,” while a third said people don’t quite understand that without bike lanes, cyclists have to risk their lives riding in traffic with other vehicles.

“It’s ridiculous… I’m 61, I don’t want to be in a roadway with cars behind me. I want a safe bike lane,” she said.

Around 10 a.m., as protesters refused to move off the platform being worked on, crews were only able to dismantle a portion of it and moved on to another section of bike lanes, leaving the area temporarily cordoned off with pylons.

In a statement Thursday, a spokesperson for Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria said the government’s position on bike lanes has not changed.

“Ontario Court of Appeal’s decision was clear, “it is illegitimate for courts to involve themselves in matters of legislative policy.” Following their decision, we announced we would restore vehicle lanes on Bloor Street West immediately,” they said.

“The people of Ontario gave our government a clear mandate to tackle the traffic that is costing our economy over $56 billion a year by removing the bike lanes on some of Toronto’s busiest streets.”

Related:

  • 2 arrests made at protest to stop Etobicoke bike lane removal

The rallies against the removal of bike lanes began Tuesday night when hundreds of protesters gathered in the area of Bloor Street West and Islington Avenue and managed to turn back work trucks that arrived to begin removing the cycling infrastructure as per the Ford government’s mandate.

At the time Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria said on X that the work was only “halted by protesters,” vowing that it will go ahead.

“Make no mistake: these bike lanes are coming out. We have a clear mandate and we will deliver,” he said.

After celebrating a short-lived victory overnight, protesters returned Wednesday morning as crews had begun preparing to dismantle the bike lanes around 11 a.m.

A stand off ensued when a lone cyclist stepped in front of a work truck to block it and was soon joined by several others.

A large police presence was on scene to ensure the work continued unobstructed, with police chief Myron Demkiw saying earlier in the day that there was no injunction against it and it was “lawful work,” which, if impeded, could lead to arrests.

Officers were heard instructing the protesters to step aside and continue their demonstration on the sidewalk and while some complied, others staged a sit-in. Police officers soon moved in and corralled the protesters onto the sidewalk, standing in a blockade in front of them to allow crews to continue the work or removing the bike lanes.

As the reflective strips and concrete barriers separating the bike lanes from the main road began being torn down, protesters continued to make a stand throughout the afternoon and into the evening, chanting “save our bike lanes” and “bike lanes save lives.”

Police arrested two people during the protest – one during the afternoon hours and another towards the evening, when construction work had halted for the day.

The first person to be arrested was a lone protester sitting on a curb barrier in a bike lane far away from the crowd that had been moved over to the sidewalk. She was instructed by police to move so that the work of removing the barriers could continue, but she did not comply. She was subsequently handcuffed and placed in a court services vehicle around 1 p.m.

Nina Thi Thi Tran, 25, from Hamilton was charged with obstruct peace officer and mischief – interfere with property – under $5,000. She is scheduled to appear in court on Jan. 8, 2027.

In the evening, shortly before 8 p.m., a second protester was arrested near Lothian Avenue and Bloor Street West. Police say they are accused of allegedly removing municipal signage and trying to leave the area.

Khoa Thanh Phan, 20, from Toronto, has been charged with mischief – interfere with lawful use of property and theft under $5,000. They are scheduled to appear in court on Jan. 7, 2027.

More to come

item.title: Public safety, housing key issues for candidates in Toronto Centre
item.dc:creator: John Marchesan
item.description: It’s the city’s smallest ward but one of the most densely populated – Toronto Centre is predicted to be a contested race between incumbent councillor Chris Moise and political newcomer Curran Stikuts, who worked as director of advocacy for the 519 Community Centre. The ward is bound by Bay Street, College Street, Yonge Street and […]
item.content:encoded:
It’s the city’s smallest ward but one of the most densely populated – Toronto Centre is predicted to be a contested race between incumbent councillor Chris Moise and political newcomer Curran Stikuts, who worked as director of advocacy for the 519 Community Centre.

The ward is bound by Bay Street, College Street, Yonge Street and Dundas Street in the west, Rosedale Valley Road, Bloor Street, Mount Pleasant Road and Charles Street in the north, the Don River and the DVP in the east, and the Esplanade and Mill Street in the south.

The ward comes with a history of serious issues that Moise says he has worked to improve over the last four years, such as high rates of homelessness, open drug use and public safety concerns.

“We had the four largest encampments in the GTA, right here in Toronto Centre,” explained Moise, a small business owner who has lived in the community for the last 30 years. “When I first got elected here I built a team of senior leadership that were able to actually house people and keep them housed.”

“I’ve been the chair of public health for the last four years and for me that’s been a priority in making sure that we support those who are the most marginalized in our community, but also making sure that the average person that lives in Toronto Centre also feels safe.”

Related:

  • 10 candidates vying to replace Gord Perks in Parkdale-High Park
  • Highly competitive race among candidates in Toronto-Danforth

But his opponents say not enough has been done in an area that encompasses some of the city’s lowest income communities neighbouring some of its most affluent, and that major changes are need to close the massive housing gap in Ward 13.

“There’s no question there are a lot of issues in Toronto Centre,” said Stikuts.

“One of the key problems we’re having is that we’re not actually having a coordinated approach. We can get folks housed in one park, in one encampment, but half the time we’re just pushing them into another.

Another challenger in the ward is Daniel Tate, the founder of the advocacy group IntegrityTO. He says what the ward needs is transparency and accountability.

“I think this is not only the change election, but this is the accountability election where people are going to have to answer for their record and they’re going to have to answer for how they treated constituents during their four years,” Tate told CityNews.

Former councillor for the ward and current NDP MPP Kristyn Wong-Tam, who backed Moise in the last election, has put her endorsement behind Stikuts.

“The fact of the matter is the disappointment is widespread and that’s why I’m proud to have the endorsement Kristyn Wong-Tam, George Smitherman, and the Toronto Labour Council,” said Stikuts.

Transit, policing and green space are also critical issues for whoever takes the seat.

Tate says lack of political experience would be an asset to constituents.

“I think that’s a benefit. I think people are looking for fresh faces, people are kind of sick and tired of career politicians and bureaucrats,” he said.

In total, there are 11 candidates running for the Ward 13 councillor seat.

item.title: Second career college court challenge reveals concerns about ‘bona fide studies’
item.dc:creator: News Staff
item.description: TORONTO — Ontario's colleges and universities ministry is alleging it could not "reliably determine bona fide studies" at two of the career colleges it barred from student financial aid — a decision those schools are now challenging in court.
item.content:encoded:
TORONTO — Ontario’s colleges and universities ministry is alleging it could not “reliably determine bona fide studies” at two of the career colleges it barred from student financial aid — a decision those schools are now challenging in court.

Two campuses of Citi College of Canadian Careers are among six schools the province blocked from the Ontario Student Assistance Program in May for the 2026-27 year, alleging “high-risk admissions” practices and other concerns.

They have filed an application in Divisional Court asking for a judicial review of that decision, similar to a court challenge by three Academy of Learning locations affected by the May order.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn did not base his decision on a “rational chain of analysis” connecting evidence to the ministry’s conclusions, and the order does not refer to any specific instances of alleged non-compliance, Citi College wrote in its court challenge.

“In making the decision, the minister reached findings regarding ‘compromised participation,’ ‘inadequate attendance tracking,’ and ‘inability to reliably determine bona fide studies’ that are not justified, transparent, or intelligible, having regard to the ministry’s own prior approvals … and the systems and safeguards Citi College had previously implemented,” the school wrote.

Citi College had been approved to administer OSAP in each of the preceding 20 years, they wrote, and two audits by the ministry last year “concluded without adverse findings.” The ministry’s allegations have not been tested or proven in court.

Quinn’s decisions to bar the six schools from receiving OSAP this year come after Career Colleges Ontario had been warning for years about possible “suspicious” OSAP activity at a small number of schools.

The minister announced last week that KPMG started an audit in August of OSAP at career colleges and he referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police based on “serious concerns” uncovered in the audit’s preliminary findings. He did not name the colleges that were the subject of the concerns referred to police.

Citi College is not aware of being subject to any issues raised by KPMG or the OPP referral, its lawyer said.

A January 2025 letter from Career Colleges Ontario to the government highlights what it calls concerning increases in OSAP usage at 10 schools, including one school that saw a nearly 2,700 per cent increase in two years. The letter was filed as part of the Academy of Learning court challenge, and all of the schools listed except for Academy of Learning are redacted, so it is not known if Citi College was included.

Data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request earlier this year shows that Citi College’s two campuses had about 133 people on OSAP in 2021-22, and three years later that rose to 1,754 students, an increase of about 1,200 per cent.

A lawyer for Citi College said in a statement Wednesday to The Canadian Press about the judicial review application that the school “continues to maintain compliance with its regulatory obligations and support its existing students in completing their programs.”

Harris Rosen also wrote in a previous statement about the OSAP increases that a more accurate calculation would use a pre-pandemic figure and rely on a compound annual growth rate, in which case Citi College would have been at about 38 per cent per year.

“The percentage increase you’ve cited appears substantial largely because it is calculated from a relatively low 2021–22 base,” Rosen wrote.

“When that figure is considered alongside the expansion of online education, broader geographic accessibility, and the relatively short duration of my client’s programs, Citi does not believe the growth is as unusual as the percentage alone may suggest.”

In the court application, Citi College argues that the minister unfairly assessed the school based on new “technological and monitoring expectations” that weren’t previously communicated to them.

Those included continuous webcam participation, long-term IP retention, forensic IP analytics, and VPN prohibitions, Citi College wrote.

When Quinn announced last week that he had referred concerns to the OPP, he said many had centred around online-only programs. This fall, the government will introduce legislation to exclude predominantly online programs at private career colleges from OSAP eligibility.

In the meantime, Quinn has also paused OSAP payments at all private post-secondary institutions.

item.title: Weekend need-to-know: Streets shut down Sunday morning for Toronto Waterfront Marathon
item.dc:creator: Meredith Bond
item.description: Runners will be taking over the streets of downtown this weekend for the Toronto Waterfront Marathon, resulting in the closure of many streets Sunday morning. Keep in mind, there is also a service adjustment on the Lakeshore West GO line. Here what’s going on this weekend. Toronto Waterfront Marathon Get out and cheer on fellow […]
item.content:encoded:
Runners will be taking over the streets of downtown this weekend for the Toronto Waterfront Marathon, resulting in the closure of many streets Sunday morning.

Keep in mind, there is also a service adjustment on the Lakeshore West GO line.

Here what’s going on this weekend.

Toronto Waterfront Marathon

Get out and cheer on fellow Torontonians this Sunday at the annual Waterfront Marathon. Over 60,000 runners are set to take to the streets, running either the full 42.2 kilometres, the half-marathon or the 5K.

More than $6 million is raised annually for the event for over 300 charities.

Details for runners, including the route and when you can pick-up your kit, are available on their website.

You can find the road closures for the event below and on the website, but expect delays in the morning in much of the downtown core and along Yonge Street.

Rugby Canada Women – Canada vs. England

Catch the Canada Women’s Rugby team in action against world champion England this weekend at BMO Field.

The women’s team will be playing their first game back on Canadian soil since they won the silver medal at the Rugby World Cup last October.

Tickets are still available for the match set to begin at 7 p.m. on Friday.

Toronto After Dark Film Festival

Watch new horror, sci-fi and action films this weekend at the Toronto After Dark Film Festival. The festival kicked off on Thursday and wll frature 14 premiers as well as 33 genre short films from Canada and around the world.

Movies will be screened Oct. 14-18, 2026, at the Scotiabank Theatre and CineCycle on Spadina.

A full lineup can be found on their website.

Fall Festival 2026 at Queen’s Park

See the beautiful colours in Queen’s Park at the annual Fall Festival on the Legislature’s grounds this Saturday. There will be a pumpkin patch and the “Almost A Farm Petting Zoo” where kids can interact with farm animals and learning about their care.

Festival-goers can also see inside the Legislative building with crafts, activities and self-guided building tours.

The event begins at 11 a.m. and runs at 4 p.m.

TTC/GO closures

Lakeshore West GO service adjustments

GO trains will run between Niagara Falls GO and Aldershot GO, and between Oakville GO and Union Station. Regularly scheduled trains that begin and end at Confederation and West Harbour GO will not run.

There will be no GO train service between Aldershot and Oakville GO due to planned construction.

GO buses will run between West Harbour/Aldershot and Oakville GO to connect to train service. There will be no GO Transit service at Appleby or Bronte GO.

Details can be found here.

Road closures

Weekend closures

Toronto Waterfront Marathon

Several road closures will be in effect for the Waterfront Marathon including rolling closures of Yonge Street and Lake Shore Boulevard. Here is a full list of the closures.

Gardiner Expressway long-term closure

As part of the long-term construction plan on the Gardiner Expressway, a stretch of the westbound Gardiner has been reduced from four lanes to three. The westbound lane closure will stretch from Park Lawn Road to Grand Avenue in southern Etobicoke. The eastbound lanes along the same stretch will be narrowed, but with no lane reductions, from April 2025 to December 2026.

For full traffic and closure updates, click here for the latest information from 680 NewsRadio Toronto.

item.title: Al Pacino to get lifetime achievement award from the Screen Actors Guild
item.dc:creator: News Staff
item.description: LOS ANGELES (AP) — Al Pacino has been named the next recipient of the SAG-AFTRA Life Achievement Award.
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Al Pacino has been named the next recipient of the SAG-AFTRA Life Achievement Award.

The 86-year-old star of “Dog Day Afternoon,” “Scent of a Woman” and a trilogy of “Godfather” films is the 62nd actor to receive the highest honor handed out by the Screen Actors Guild -American Federation of Television and Radio Artists.

“I wondered and wandered most of my life but have always felt at home with a script and my fellow actors. It’s the work and the actors along the way that have been among the greatest joys of my life,” Pacino said in a statement Thursday. “It’s an honor to be recognized by SAG-AFTRA in celebrating the journey.”

He’ll pick up the prize on Feb. 28 at the 33rd annual Actor Awards at the Shrine Auditorium in Los Angeles. The show will stream live on Netflix.

The award also honors humanitarian work, and the guild cited Pacino’s charitable efforts for disaster relief, fighting hunger and poverty and his support for local theater companies, including the Shakespeare Center of Los Angeles.

The native New Yorker was a young actor best known for his stage work when director Francis Ford Coppola tapped him to play Michael Corleone in 1972’s “The Godfather” against the wishes of a studio that wanted an established star in the coveted part.

He would be nominated for an Oscar for the role and become regarded as one of the finest actors of his generation. He got annual Academy Award nominations for the next three years, for “Serpico,” “The Godfather Part II” and “Dog Day Afternoon.” He would not win until he took best actor for “Scent of a Woman” in 1993, a year when he was also nominated for supporting actor for “Glengarry Glen Ross.” He’s been nominated nine times overall, most recently in 2020 for “The Irishman.”

Pacino has also won two competitive Actor Awards from SAG-AFTRA, two Emmys, four Golden Globes and the Globes’ lifetime achievement honor, the Cecil B. DeMille Award.

“I have spent my life in awe and appreciation of the force of nature that is Al Pacino,” SAG-AFTRA President Sean Astin said in a statement. “When you watch him perform, you are witnessing a student and a master. Al Pacino is an artist of extraordinary courage, intensity and heart whose work has always set an exceptional standard of skill and talent. All of that and he’s just plain fun to watch.”

The SAG-AFTRA Life Achievement Award dates to 1962. Previous winners include Barbara Stanwyck, James Stewart, Pearl Bailey, Frank Sinatra, James Cagney, Katharine Hepburn, Audrey Hepburn, Paul Newman, James Earl Jones, Jane Fonda and Harrison Ford.

Andrew Dalton, The Associated Press

item.title: Trump, after bipartisan backlash, says Pentagon won’t livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter
item.dc:creator: News Staff
item.description: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Thursday that the Pentagon will no longer livestream the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan, after the announcement faced bipartisan criticism and Vice President JD Vance said he wouldn’t watch it.
item.content:encoded:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Thursday that the Pentagon will no longer livestream the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan, after the announcement faced bipartisan criticism and Vice President JD Vance said he wouldn’t watch it.

Trump said on social media that publicly airing the execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan.”

But, he continued, “many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device.”

The Pentagon has said Hasan’s execution is scheduled for Dec. 3. Trump said the execution can be viewed in person by immediate families of the victims, “if they so choose.”

The announcement earlier this month from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that Hasan’s execution would be public — and subsequent confirmation from the Pentagon that it would be livestreamed — prompted significant blowback from both Republicans and Democrats, with many pointing out that the images could be used to fuel radicalization.

Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell said Trump and Hegseth discussed the decision to drop the livestream plans before the president’s announcement on social media.

“The Secretary supports the President’s decision, and they are completely aligned,” Parnell said.

When asked how the public execution comported with his Christian faith earlier this month, Vance said “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen.”

“So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Vance said, adding: “Now, that said, I mean, look, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it.”

Vance is Catholic, and the church has long opposed capital punishment. The head of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops had condemned the Trump administration’s decision to livestream Hasan’s execution, with Archbishop Paul S. Coakley saying the move was a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered.”

Other top Republicans, including House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., voiced similar sentiments.

For his part, the president has defended his decision to approve the use of a firing squad, but had for days distanced himself from Hegseth’s announcement that it would be public.

“Well, they’re making a determination about that,” Trump said Friday when asked about the livestream. As for Hasan and the method of execution, Trump said then: “He will be killed. He will be, through firing squad. I really don’t care how he goes, as long as he goes. And I think the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him.”

Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building on Nov. 5, 2009, where soldiers were waiting in long lines to receive immunizations and medical clearance for deployment. He shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He also shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.

Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defense during his 2013 trial. Hasan was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement and now uses a wheelchair.

Hasan could seek a lengthy delay of his execution, though given his behavior at trial, he may not want to.

The U.S. military hasn’t executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.

——-

Associated Press writer Konstantin Toropin contributed to this report.

Seung Min Kim, The Associated Press

item.title: SeatGeek Canada hit with more fines totalling $22,500 over ticket resale violations
item.dc:creator: News Staff
item.description: TORONTO — SeatGeek Canada is facing two more fines from the Ontario government for allegedly contravening a recent law capping the sale of event tickets at face value.
item.content:encoded:
TORONTO — SeatGeek Canada is facing two more fines from the Ontario government for allegedly contravening a recent law capping the sale of event tickets at face value.

The province’s consumer beware website shows the new fines issued to the ticket resale platform earlier this month total $22,500 collectively.

The website says the first of the two fines amounts to $15,000 and is for allegedly making a ticket available for sale or facilitating a sale of a seat beyond the resale price limit.

The second fine is for $7,500 and is for allegedly failing to disclose the total price of a ticket when a seat was purchased from a primary seller.

SeatGeek Canada did not immediately respond to questions about what events the fines stem from or whether it will fight the penalties.

Giulia Paikin, a spokesperson for the Ontario Minister of Public and Business Service Delivery Stephen Crawford, also did not answer questions about the nature of the penalties.

However, she sent a statement that repeated nearly verbatim what the province has previously said about anyone responsible for price cap violations facing fines of up to $250,000.

“We will not hesitate to hold bad actors who break the rules accountable,” an email from Paikin said.

SeatGeek’s new fines stem from legislation the province implemented earlier this year, after fans complained about resale prices for tickets to Taylor Swift’s Eras tour in 2024 and last year’s playoff run by the Toronto Blue Jays.

The legislation was meant to keep people from reselling seats to Ontario events for well beyond face value and tamp down on scalpers profiting off their ability to scoop up tickets to hot concerts and shows.

After the legislation came into effect, the province issued $25,000 in fines to SeatGeek in August for similar offences.

A $20,000 fine for fellow resale website StubHub Canada followed in September.

When SeatGeek was given its first round of fines, it told The Canadian Press it had notified third-party sellers on its platform about the new law but was still seeking guidance from the province around how to comply with the regulations.

The platform argued it is challenging to confirm the original value of tickets because many sellers don’t have access to that information. Sometimes seats have changed hands several times before they wind up on a resale site and if tickets were bought as part of a broader package, like a season’s seat arrangement, it can be hard to break down the value of a single ticket.

To address these issues, SeatGeek said it has asked Ontario to define what counts as acceptable proof of a ticket’s original price and for guidance around how a marketplace is expected to validate the cost of seats.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

item.title: Supreme Court will hear appeal affecting Ottawa’s single-use plastics ban
item.dc:creator: News Staff
item.description: OTTAWA — The Supreme Court of Canada said Thursday it will hear an appeal that will determine if Ottawa's ban on single-use plastics can remain in place.
item.content:encoded:
OTTAWA — The Supreme Court of Canada said Thursday it will hear an appeal that will determine if Ottawa’s ban on single-use plastics can remain in place.

In 2022, Ottawa phased in a ban on the manufacture and sale of six single-use plastic items, including straws, stir sticks, cutlery, takeout containers and the six-pack rings used to hold soda and beer cans.

The government said at the time it chose those items because they were commonly found in litter and had known and accessible alternatives.

In order to introduce the ban, the federal government listed “plastic manufactured items” as toxic under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, following a scientific assessment.

In 2023, the Federal Court said that listing was too broad, in part because the federal government had failed to demonstrate that all plastic items harm human health or the environment.

The Federal Court of Appeal overturned the lower court’s decision in January, allowing the federal government to keep the ban in place. The three-judge panel unanimously ruled the decision to list plastic manufactured items as toxic was reasonable.

They argued the lower court had erred by viewing as one step what was actually a two-step process: designating plastics as toxic under the Act and regulating individual plastic items.

The initial decision to list all plastics as toxic was challenged by a group representing companies in Canada’s plastics industry, along with three chemical companies which manufacture plastics.

The plastics industry argued, among other things, that a lack of testing to determine which plastics are harmful made Ottawa’s decision unreasonable.

The Court of Appeal dismissed that argument in January.

“To put the matter bluntly … the chemical content of (plastics) is irrelevant to the sea otter choking on a plastic straw. The problem is the plastic item itself, not its chemistry,” the judges wrote.

Karen Wirsig, senior program manager for plastics at Environmental Defence, said until the Supreme Court rules, Ottawa should maintain the ban.

“It is rare for appeals to be granted so we were not particularly expecting it. However, it does open the opportunity for a stronger precedent for the listing from the Supreme Court of Canada,” Wirsig told The Canadian Press.

The group representing plastics companies has not yet responded to a request for comment.

This report from The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

Nick Murray, The Canadian Press

item.title: Human trafficking survivor faced with tax debt plans petition to change federal legislation
item.dc:creator: Dee Burman
item.description: A Toronto human trafficking survivor is increasing her push to change federal law to better address the financial struggles people like her face by launching a House of Commons petition and her efforts to do so have recently cleared a huge hurdle. Late last month, CityNews reported on Cassandra Harvey’s years-long battle with the Canada […]
item.content:encoded:
A Toronto human trafficking survivor is increasing her push to change federal law to better address the financial struggles people like her face by launching a House of Commons petition and her efforts to do so have recently cleared a huge hurdle.

Late last month, CityNews reported on Cassandra Harvey’s years-long battle with the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) over benefits claimed in her name by her trafficker.

“During COVID, my trafficker started claiming the CERB benefits and also claimed a large portion of my child tax benefit,” she previously told Speakers Corner.

Harvey says despite sending what she calls “overwhelming proof” to the CRA that she was a trafficking victim who did not personally benefit from any of those tax decisions, the agency is still calling for her to pay some of that back.

“Because of that, for years now, they’ve clawed back on my tax returns. They’ve clawed back on all my child tax benefits, my GST, HST,” Harvey said.

Since our report aired, Harvey has heard from several other victims facing the same troubles.

“I am not alone but as far as I know I am the only one legally challenging this issue because I am able to do so, many others are not,” she said.

Harvey hired Alex Klyguine, a lawyer with Ottawa based Taxpayer Law, who says it’s been a slow process so far to get the CRA to forgive the debt.

“What we’re asking for is a remission order which gives relief from all amounts outstanding,” he explained.

“The problem with remission orders is they are seldom granted.”

 He says there needs to be a change in federal legislation which currently does not specifically address CRA debts owed by survivors whose identities were also stolen.

“Federally, I think that there’s still a gap and there is still room to create a piece of legislation that prevents those debts from being collected on,” he said.

That’s a big part of Harvey’s House of Commons petition which received support from M.P. Danielle Martin this week and has approved it for online publication.

“We understand the issues raised in this petition are very important and distressing for anyone who is rebuilding their life after enduring any form of violence,” a spokesperson for Martin said.

Once published, Harvey will begin to gather the required amount of signatures for the petition to be presented for consideration.

“But it’s ultimately up to the parliament and we’re hoping that the members of the federal parliament are able to see this issue as important enough to warrant action on their behalf,” Klyguine added.

When CityNews contacted the CRA about Harvey’s case a spokesperson said they cannot comment, citing privacy laws.

“The CRA takes cases involving vulnerable individuals, especially those impacted by coercion or exploitation, with the utmost seriousness,”  the spokesperson said. 

“The CRA is committed to reaching a resolution while carefully assessing each victim’s circumstances.”
